analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. drug prices at the average of what six other wealthy nations pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it sat without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for drug and biologic makers to charge Americans a higher list price than the average list price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Companies would have to report their prices in each country to the government every year, and any unit sold above the cap would draw a penalty of ten times the price difference. This targets the well-documented gap between U.S. drug prices and what the same drugs cost abroad.
analysis.who_benefits: American patients who pay full or partly out-of-pocket prices for brand-name drugs and biologics, since list prices are the anchor for copays, coinsurance, and uninsured purchases. Lower list prices would also flow to employer plans and insurers that base cost-sharing on list prices. Seniors paying for expensive biologics would be among the clearest gainers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying out-of-pocket for brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: Caps the U.S. retail list price of every covered drug and biologic at the average list price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom [S2][S3].

Imposes a civil monetary penalty of ten times the price difference for each unit sold above the cap, giving companies a strong financial reason to comply rather than just absorb occasional fines [S3].
Requires manufacturers to report list prices in the U.S. and all six reference countries annually, so the government could compute the cap without relying on opaque pricing data [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and biologic manufacturers, whose U.S. list prices for drugs that currently cost more in America than in the six reference countries would fall toward the international average. Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers might also see lower upstream costs, but the direct cost falls on the makers of patented medicines.

drawbacks.text: Price controls pegged to foreign prices could reduce revenue for new medicines, and the standard objection is that this would lead companies to invest less in researching future drugs, especially small-patient-population biologics where development costs are high. The bill text contains no offsetting incentives to replace that lost revenue [S3].

Enforcement rests entirely on prices reported by the manufacturers themselves each year, backed only by review of public filings, so the accuracy of the cap depends on companies reporting honestly [S3].

The cap applies to list prices, not the net prices after rebates and discounts that insurers actually pay, so the real-world savings for patients depend on how list prices translate into what people pay at the pharmacy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people paying U.S. list prices today, the benefit is direct and large: American list prices often run several times what the same drugs sell for in the six reference countries. The main cost is a slower pipeline of new drugs if research funding shrinks, a real risk but one spread over years and hard to quantify. The bill is simple and enforceable on its face, though it relies on self-reported price data and does not address the list-versus-net price gap. On balance, the benefit to patients paying today's prices outweighs the acknowledged risk to future innovation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in April 2023, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no cosponsors, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion House action during the 118th Congress [S5][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug and biologic manufacturers, who keep charging U.S. prices above what the same drugs cost in peer nations; no patient saw a change.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only sponsorship; no further committee or floor action was available to him as a non-committee leader.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where each party stood; it was introduced by a Republican with zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force U.S. list prices down to the average of six peer countries, with a penalty of ten times the price difference per unit sold above the cap. Because American patients pay some of the highest drug prices in the world, the industry's higher U.S. profits come directly out of patients' pockets.

Lower list prices would cut the upstream cost of brand-name drugs these intermediaries purchase and price cost-sharing against, but they could also see narrower rebate spreads if the list-price-to-net-price gap shrinks. The bill does not regulate them directly.
